newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: AUSTRALIA DEBT YIELD CURVE STEEPENS ON MACFARLANE.
newsitem.headline: AUSTRALIA DEBT YIELD CURVE STEEPENS ON MACFARLANE.

text.p: *Short Australian debt futures were firm following comments by RBA governor Macfarlane on Tuesday, while the long end remained dogged by a fragile U.S. Treasury market.
*U.S. July retail sales due later on Wednesday.
Short Australian debt futures firmed in early trading after a less hawkish than expected speech by Reserve Bank governor Ian Macfarlane late on Tuesday.

Macfarlane said the RBA did not have a growth ceiling and that the economy could grow 4.5 percent or more over the next few years without sparking inflation. He also did not see that monetary policy is placing any contraint on growth.

"The whole tenor of the speech is the bank intends to hold rates where they are for a long period of time, and there is still an outside risk that they might lower them again," said Stephen Roberts, chief econmist at UBS Australia.

"There is no pressure on them as far as they can see to start to tighten. The short end is well protected with cash rates being no higher than 5.0 percent this of side of mid-1998 and probably end-1998," Roberts added.
The September bill futures contract touched a high of 95.08 in early trading equating to a cash rate of 4.92 percent compared to current 5.0 percent official rates.
Meanwhile, the long end of the curve was dogged again by a fragile U.S. Treasury market, which is fearing the worst from the release of the July retail sales report later on Wednesday.
Sales are expected to rise 0.7 percent on average, although the forecast range is from 0.5 to 1.2 percent, according to a Reuters survey of economists.

Although current local fundamentals are superior to that of the U.S., analysts said all the good news has been priced in, leaving the long-end vulnerable to further downward pressure on U.S. Treasuries.

The yield curve steepened sharply as the short-end outperformed against longer maturities, and also outpaced the rest of the dollar bloc. In his speech, Macfarlane noted that Australian rates were lower than the U.S. out to five years which he felt was "entirely fit and proper".
